samasa.sense: a sound that broke the spirit of the asura armies

morph.note: Periphrastic perfect of the causative पूरय- ‘to fill’: पूरय- + आम् + आस.

विधायिन् is वि + √धा with the kṛt affix -इन् (ṇini), ‘one who brings about’; instrumental singular -इना. The genitive समस्तदैत्यसैन्यानाम् is construed with तेजः, the first member of this compound — a construction the epic style allows.
Accusative plural of the feminine consonant stem ककुभ्, ‘region, quarter of the sky’.

mantras.anvaya: (देवी) समस्तदैत्यसैन्यानां तेजोवधविधायिना निजघण्टास्वनेन च ककुभः पूरयामास।
mantras.anvaya_en: The subject (the Devī) carries over from 9.19. The verb पूरयामास has ककुभः as object and निजघण्टास्वनेन as instrument; the long qualifier with its genitive says what the bell’s sound does.
mantras.lit: And with the sound of her own bell, which brought about the destruction of the vigour of all the Daitya armies, she filled the quarters.
mantras.tr: And she filled every quarter of the sky with the ringing of her bell, a sound that drained the strength of all the Daitya hosts.

comm.t: The bell is the third of the Devī’s sounds. Its power is named exactly: it destroys the तेजस् — the fire, vigour or spirit — of the enemy armies.

The text says the same of the bell elsewhere: it was Indra’s gift, taken from Airāvata (2.22); its sound stupefies the asuras (2.56); and in the Nārāyaṇī hymn the devotee prays to the bell that ‘destroys the tejas of the Daityas’ (हिनस्ति दैत्यतेजांसि, 11.27). The bell rung in worship is understood in this light in Śākta practice.

samasa.vigraha: महान्तः च ते नादाः च, तैः
त्याजितः इभानां महामदः यैः ते, तैः
samasa.type: bahuvrīhi (its second member इभमहामद is a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, इभानां महामदः, and महामद a karmadhāraya, महान् मदः)
samasa.literal: by which the great rut of the elephants was made to be abandoned
samasa.sense: roars that broke the frenzy of the war-elephants
samasa.alt: Also analysable as त्याजिताः इभाः महामदं यैः ते, ‘by which the elephants were made to give up their great rut’; with a causative both persons and things can be its objects, and the sense is the same.

morph.note: त्याजित is the past participle of the causative of √त्यज् (त्याजय- ‘make give up’): ‘made to be abandoned’.
Irregular accusative singular of गो, which means ‘cow’ and, in verse, ‘the earth’.
As in 9.20; the repetition links the lion’s roar to the Devī’s bell.

mantras.anvaya: ततः सिंहः त्याजितेभमहामदैः महानादैः गगनं गां तथा एव दश दिशः पूरयामास।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject सिंहः, instrument महानादैः with its qualifier, verb पूरयामास, and three objects: गगनम्, गाम्, दश दिशः.
mantras.lit: Then the lion, with great roars which made the elephants give up their great rut, filled the sky, the earth and likewise the ten directions.
mantras.tr: Then the lion filled the sky, the earth and all ten directions with thunderous roars that broke the frenzy of the war-elephants.

comm.t: The Devī’s lion adds its roar to her sounds. Elephants in rut (मद) are at their most dangerous; the lion’s roar makes them lose it — a conventional image of the lion as the elephant’s master, here aimed at the asura war-elephants.
The ‘ten directions’ are the eight points of the compass with the zenith and the nadir: the roar fills all of space.

samasa.sense: by the crash of her blow

morph.note: Absolutive with two prefixes, सम् + उद् + √पत्: ‘having flown up, leaping up’.
हित is the past participle of √धा; with the gati तिरस् ‘aside, out of sight’, तिरोहित means ‘hidden, put out of sight’, here ‘drowned out’. It serves as the main verb.
Adverb (from प्राञ्च्) used attributively: प्राक् स्वनाः ‘the sounds of before’. It could also be read as the first member of a compound प्राक्स्वनाः; the sense is the same.

mantras.anvaya: ततः काली समुत्पत्य कराभ्यां गगनं क्ष्माम् (च) अताडयत्; तन्निनादेन ते प्राक् स्वनाः तिरोहिताः।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences. Kālī’s action (… अताडयत्), with two objects in asyndeton, as गगनं गाम् in 9.21; then the effect (ते … तिरोहिताः), with तन्निनादेन as cause.
mantras.lit: Then Kālī, leaping up, struck the sky and the earth with her two hands; by the din of that, those earlier sounds were drowned out.
mantras.tr: Then Kālī leapt up and struck the sky and the earth with both her hands, and the crash of it drowned every sound that had gone before.

comm.t: Kālī — the fierce form who sprang from the Devī’s brow in chapter 7 and drank Raktabīja’s blood in chapter 8 — makes the loudest sound of all, and the conch, bowstring, bell and lion’s roar (9.19–21) are lost in it.
In the Gita Press pāṭha Kālī here is the same as Cāmuṇḍā (named so at 7.25 after killing Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa); the text uses the two names interchangeably in the uttama carita.

flags.uncertain: गगनम् is taken as a second object of अताडयत् (‘struck the sky and the earth’), in parallel with गगनं गाम् in 9.21. It can also be the goal of समुत्पत्य (‘leaping up into the sky, she struck the earth’).
